title: Is it possible to develop a tutor-proof test?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou examines whether it's possible to design a "tutor-proof" selection test -- one immune to coaching by parents and paid tutors -- and concludes the concept doesn't hold up. She traces the appeal of curriculum-neutral formats like non-verbal reasoning tests, which research by economists such as David Card suggests can help identify talented but disadvantaged students in low-stakes, government-run settings. But in high-stakes selection for prestigious schools, she argues, the same "tutor-proof" label that sounds protective actually functions as a challenge to well-resourced tutors, who reliably find ways to coach even ostensibly novel question types. Drawing on the well-established "practice effect" from cognitive psychology, she explains that near transfer between similar question types is real even when far transfer is hard, so small tutoring-driven gains can decide high-stakes outcomes, and that constantly generating genuinely new question types to stay ahead of tutors runs into real technical limits and skips proper validation. She also invokes Goodhart's Law, illustrating with the example of early AI essay-marking tools that turned out to reward essay length rather than quality, to show how any measure that becomes a target eventually loses its meaning. Christodoulou concludes that practice effects are not a bug to engineer away but the entire point of education, and that the better project is designing tests worth teaching to rather than tests immune to teaching.
points: The core argument is that "tutor-proof" is an unstable concept because of the well-established practice effect: practicing a specific skill reliably improves performance on that skill, so any coachable format eventually yields to sustained, well-resourced tutoring.

Non-verbal reasoning tests can help identify talented, disadvantaged students in low-stakes, large-scale government contexts (per David Card's research), but that same rationale collapses under the intense, sustained tutoring pressure of high-stakes selective-school entry.

Constantly manufacturing genuinely novel question types to outrun tutors runs into hard technical limits and forces test developers to skip the multi-year validation process good assessment design requires.

Christodoulou's Goodhart's Law example -- early AI essay markers that turned out to just reward essay length -- shows how any measure, once it becomes a target that students and tutors optimize for, stops measuring what it was built to measure.

Her reframe is that practice effects aren't a design flaw to eliminate but "why education works": a good assessment should promote practice of genuinely valuable skills rather than trying to dodge coachability altogether.
quotes: If you are using a test as a selection mechanism for a prestigious institution, you will have armies of very smart parents and well-paid tutors trying to crack the code of the test.

David Card is a Nobel laureate who has done research showing that a non-verbal test administered at second grade in a district in Florida "led to large increases in the fractions of economically disadvantaged and minority students placed in gifted programs.
The practice effect is one of the most robust findings in cognitive psychology, and poses an enormous challenge to the idea of the tutor-proof test.

If you are running 3 test sessions a year, after ten years you will need to come up with thirty different types of question. There are limits to how many ways you can vary the essential concept of looking at a 2D shape and moving it around in some way.

A really famous one is that early AI essay markers delivered pretty good levels of agreement with human markers, and seemed to have solved the problem of AI marking. However, on closer investigation it turned out that they were largely just rewarding the length of the essay.

When you stop and think about it, the concept of the tutor-proof test does not really hold water. Of course you get better at something if you practice it. That is a good thing, and that is why education works!

A good assessment should promote practice of the valuable things. It shouldn't remove the valuable things and replace them with less valuable things, on the grounds that some students will get more practice of the valuable things.
